opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a reasonable starting point, but on its own I don't find it all that illuminating. The problem is that almost anything can be described as achieving goals if you squint at it the right way. A thermostat "achieves the goal" of keeping a room at a certain temperature. A bacterium swims toward glucose. A chess program achieves the goal of checkmating its opponent. So if intelligence is just goal achievement, it becomes a very broad notion that doesn't distinguish what's interesting about human or animal intelligence from what a simple feedback mechanism does.

What I find more useful is to ask *how* a system achieves its goals and *under what range of circumstances*. Can it achieve them in situations it's never encountered before? Can it form abstractions and analogies, carry what it learned in one context over to a very different one? Can it figure out what the goals even should be when the situation is ambiguous? Living things, and humans especially, are remarkable at this kind of flexible adaptation. A lot of our AI systems achieve goals very impressively within the distribution they were trained on, but they can be surprisingly brittle when you move them a little outside of it.

There's also the question of where the goals come from. In biological organisms, goals emerge from the organism's own needs: survival, reproduction, social life, curiosity. In AI systems, the goals are almost always given to them by us, specified in an objective function or a prompt. That's a pretty big difference, and it's part of why I'm cautious about simply mapping the same definition onto both.

So I'd say "capacity to achieve goals" is one dimension of intelligence, but it's not sufficient. Intelligence isn't a single thing you can put on one scale. It's a collection of capacities, and generalization, understanding, and adaptability are the parts that really matter when we compare living systems to machines.

r001.rationale: The response says a bacterium and many other systems can be described as achieving goals, but it does not state that every living thing therefore has some degree of intelligence.

r002.rationale: It calls goal achievement alone too broad and unilluminating because it fails to distinguish human or animal intelligence from simple mechanisms, while discussing AI systems in that context.

r003.rationale: It explicitly raises the question of where goals come from.

r004.rationale: It contrasts goals emerging from biological organisms’ needs with AI goals being supplied by people through objectives or prompts.

r005.rationale: The response notes a difference between biological and AI goals and says it is cautious about applying the same definition to both, but does not clearly state that conflating these senses makes AI intelligence harder to discuss.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's useful as a starting point, but it hides a lot. The appeal of "intelligence is the capacity to achieve goals" is that it's substrate-neutral. You can apply it to a bacterium swimming up a nutrient gradient, to a crow solving a puzzle, to a chess program. It gets us out of the trap of defining intelligence as "whatever humans do." And it's the definition a lot of the AI field has implicitly adopted, going back to the idea of rational agents maximizing expected utility.

But where I think it falls short is that it treats "goals" as if they were given, as if they were just inputs to the system. In living things, goals aren't handed down. They emerge from the organism's needs, from staying alive, from being embedded in an environment and a body. A huge part of what we mean by intelligence in animals is figuring out what to want in a situation, what to pay attention to, what the actual problem is. The goal-achievement definition skips over all of that and jumps straight to optimization.

With AI systems, this gets tricky in a different way. When we say a chess program has the goal of winning, we're really describing our goal, which we baked into the objective function. The system has no stake in it. So the definition can mislead us into attributing a kind of agency that isn't there, or into thinking that a system that scores well on some objective "understands" what it's doing. We've seen over and over that systems can achieve a goal we specified while completely missing the thing we actually cared about. That's the whole story of shortcut learning and benchmark gaming.

The other thing I'd push on is that intelligence, at least in the biological sense, seems to be deeply about flexibility and generalization. It's not just achieving a goal, it's achieving a goal in situations you haven't seen before, with limited data, by making analogies to things you do know. A thermostat achieves a goal. We don't want to call it intelligent, and if we do, the word stops being useful. So you end up having to add all these qualifiers, and at that point the clean definition isn't doing much work anymore.

So I'd say it's a fine operational definition for building systems, and a poor one for understanding what intelligence actually is. I'm honestly skeptical that any one-sentence definition will do it. I think of intelligence more as a cluster of capacities, and which ones matter depends on what question you're asking.

r001.rationale: It gives a bacterium and other examples, but does not state that every living thing therefore has some degree of intelligence.

r002.rationale: It argues that the definition can mislead when assessing AI, uses a thermostat as an example of excessive breadth, and says the definition is poor for understanding intelligence.

r003.rationale: It explains that AI goals are baked in by people, but does not ask where AI systems’ goals come from.

r004.rationale: It contrasts goals emerging from living organisms’ needs with an AI system’s goal being specified by people, with no stake for the system itself.

r005.rationale: It says treating an AI’s specified objective as its own goal can mislead us into attributing agency or understanding, conveying the difficulty this creates when discussing AI intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful as a starting point, but it leaves a lot unspecified. What counts as a goal? Whose goals are we talking about? Evolution has produced organisms that do remarkably sophisticated things, but we don’t necessarily want to say that they’re explicitly representing a goal and figuring out how to achieve it.

And with AI, a system can be extremely good at achieving a particular goal—winning a game, for example—and still be unable to cope with a small change in the task. So I’m interested in what that definition leaves out: how flexibly you can adapt, how you make sense of a new situation, and how you bring what you’ve learned to bear on something you haven’t encountered before. Goal achievement is part of the picture, but by itself it doesn’t tell us very much about the kind of intelligence a system has.

r001.rationale: It says organisms can act sophisticatedly without explicitly representing goals, but does not state that every living thing has some degree of intelligence.

r002.rationale: It calls the definition a useful starting point that leaves things unspecified, but does not judge it too broad for assessing systems such as GPT-3.

r003.rationale: It asks whose goals are involved, but does not ask where AI systems' goals come from.

r004.rationale: It contrasts organisms with AI performing a task, but does not clearly distinguish what having a goal means for a living person versus an AI system such as AlphaGo.

r005.rationale: It says goal achievement alone reveals little about a system's intelligence, but does not state that conflating biological and AI senses of goals makes AI intelligence harder to discuss.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful as a starting point, but it leaves a lot unspecified. What kinds of goals? In what kinds of environments? A thermostat achieves a goal, in some sense, but we don’t usually want to call it intelligent. And a system can be extremely good at achieving one particular goal while being completely helpless when the situation changes.

With living things, there’s also the question of where the goals come from. We have goals related to survival, but we also form new goals, explore, and try to understand things without necessarily having a particular outcome in mind. In AI, we typically supply the goal, and then measure how well the system optimizes for it.

So I’m more interested in the capacities that make flexible behavior possible: learning, forming abstractions, using what you know in a new situation. Defining intelligence as achieving goals doesn’t really tell us how to distinguish that flexibility from success on a narrowly specified task.

r001.rationale: The response discusses goals in living things but does not say that every living thing therefore has some degree of intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says goal achievement leaves key distinctions unspecified and cannot distinguish flexible intelligence from success on a narrow task, making the definition inadequate for assessing AI systems.

r003.rationale: It says AI goals are typically supplied, but does not ask where AI systems’ goals come from.

r004.rationale: It contrasts living things’ survival and self-formed goals with AI systems’ supplied goals, expressing different meanings of having a goal.

r005.rationale: The response distinguishes living and AI goals, but does not state that conflating those senses makes discussing AI intelligence harder.
